The **2013 Australian federal election in New South Wales** was held on **7 September 2013** as part of the national election that brought the **Liberal–National Coalition**, led by **Tony Abbott**, to government and ended the second Rudd/Gillard/Rudd Labor government.

New South Wales was the largest electoral prize in the country, with **48 House of Representatives seats** and **6 Senate vacancies** being contested.

---

## Overall result in New South Wales

### House of Representatives

The Coalition won a strong victory in NSW.

| Party/group | Seats won in NSW |
|---|---:|
| Liberal Party | 23 |
| National Party | 7 |
| Australian Labor Party | 18 |
| Greens | 0 |
| Independents/Others | 0 |
| **Total** | **48** |

So the Coalition won **30 of 48 NSW lower-house seats**, while Labor won **18**.

The Coalition made substantial gains from Labor, especially in western Sydney, the Central Coast and regional NSW.

---

## Two-party-preferred vote in NSW

On the two-party-preferred vote, NSW voted clearly for the Coalition.

| Party | Two-party-preferred vote |
|---|---:|
| Liberal/National Coalition | about **54.3%** |
| Labor | about **45.7%** |

This represented a swing to the Coalition compared with the 2010 election.

---

## Primary vote in NSW

Approximate NSW House of Representatives primary vote:

| Party/group | Primary vote share |
|---|---:|
| Liberal/National Coalition | about **47%** |
| Labor | about **34%** |
| Greens | about **8%** |
| Palmer United Party | about **4%** |
| Others/Independents | remainder |

The Coalition’s primary vote was particularly strong in outer-suburban Sydney, regional NSW and traditional Liberal seats on Sydney’s North Shore and eastern suburbs.

---

# House of Representatives results by electorate

NSW had **48 federal divisions** at the 2013 election.

## Seats won by the Liberal Party

| Electorate | Winning candidate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Banks | David Coleman | Liberal gain from Labor |
| Barton | Nickolas Varvaris | Liberal gain from Labor |
| Bennelong | John Alexander | Liberal retained |
| Berowra | Philip Ruddock | Liberal retained |
| Bradfield | Paul Fletcher | Liberal retained |
| Cook | Scott Morrison | Liberal retained |
| Eden-Monaro | Peter Hendy | Liberal gain from Labor |
| Farrer | Sussan Ley | Liberal retained |
| Gilmore | Ann Sudmalis | Liberal retained after Joanna Gash retired |
| Hughes | Craig Kelly | Liberal retained |
| Hume | Angus Taylor | Liberal retained after Alby Schultz retired |
| Lindsay | Fiona Scott | Liberal gain from Labor |
| Macarthur | Russell Matheson | Liberal retained |
| Mackellar | Bronwyn Bishop | Liberal retained |
| Mitchell | Alex Hawke | Liberal retained |
| North Sydney | Joe Hockey | Liberal retained |
| Paterson | Bob Baldwin | Liberal retained |
| Reid | Craig Laundy | Liberal gain from Labor |
| Robertson | Lucy Wicks | Liberal gain from Labor |
| Warringah | Tony Abbott | Liberal retained; Abbott became Prime Minister |
| Wentworth | Malcolm Turnbull | Liberal retained |

The Liberal Party’s NSW performance was especially notable in **western Sydney**, where it won seats such as **Banks, Barton, Lindsay and Reid**, and in bellwether or marginal seats such as **Eden-Monaro** and **Robertson**.

---

## Seats won by the National Party

| Electorate | Winning candidate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Calare | John Cobb | Nationals retained |
| Cowper | Luke Hartsuyker | Nationals retained |
| Lyne | David Gillespie | Nationals gain from Independent-held seat |
| New England | Barnaby Joyce | Nationals gain from Independent-held seat |
| Page | Kevin Hogan | Nationals gain from Labor |
| Parkes | Mark Coulton | Nationals retained |
| Riverina | Michael McCormack | Nationals retained |

Two of the most important National Party results were:

- **New England**: Barnaby Joyce moved from the Senate to the House of Representatives and won the seat after independent MP **Tony Windsor** retired.
- **Lyne**: David Gillespie won the seat after independent MP **Rob Oakeshott** retired.

Both Windsor and Oakeshott had supported the Gillard Labor minority government after the 2010 election, so their retirements and the return of those seats to the Nationals were politically significant.

---

## Seats won by Labor

| Electorate | Winning candidate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Blaxland | Jason Clare | Labor retained |
| Charlton | Pat Conroy | Labor retained after Greg Combet retired |
| Chifley | Ed Husic | Labor retained |
| Cunningham | Sharon Bird | Labor retained |
| Fowler | Chris Hayes | Labor retained |
| Grayndler | Anthony Albanese | Labor retained |
| Greenway | Michelle Rowland | Labor retained |
| Hunter | Joel Fitzgibbon | Labor retained |
| Kingsford Smith | Matt Thistlethwaite | Labor retained after Peter Garrett retired |
| McMahon | Chris Bowen | Labor retained |
| Newcastle | Sharon Claydon | Labor retained after Sharon Grierson retired |
| Parramatta | Julie Owens | Labor retained |
| Richmond | Justine Elliot | Labor retained |
| Shortland | Jill Hall | Labor retained |
| Sydney | Tanya Plibersek | Labor retained |
| Throsby | Stephen Jones | Labor retained |
| Watson | Tony Burke | Labor retained |
| Werriwa | Laurie Ferguson | Labor retained |

Labor’s NSW representation was concentrated in:

- inner Sydney,
- western and south-western Sydney,
- the Illawarra,
- Newcastle/Hunter,
- and the far north coast seat of **Richmond**.

---

# Seats that changed hands in NSW

The Coalition made major gains in NSW.

## Liberal gains from Labor

| Seat | New member | Previous party |
|---|---|---|
| Banks | David Coleman | Labor |
| Barton | Nickolas Varvaris | Labor |
| Eden-Monaro | Peter Hendy | Labor |
| Lindsay | Fiona Scott | Labor |
| Reid | Craig Laundy | Labor |
| Robertson | Lucy Wicks | Labor |

## National gain from Labor

| Seat | New member | Previous party |
|---|---|---|
| Page | Kevin Hogan | Labor |

## National gains from Independents

| Seat | New member | Previous member |
|---|---|---|
| Lyne | David Gillespie | Rob Oakeshott, Independent |
| New England | Barnaby Joyce | Tony Windsor, Independent |

## Liberal gain in Dobell

| Seat | New member | Previous situation |
|---|---|---|
| Dobell | Karen McNamara | Previously held by Craig Thomson, originally Labor, later Independent |

Dobell was a high-profile contest because of controversy surrounding sitting MP **Craig Thomson**, who had left the Labor Party and contested the election as an independent. The Liberal candidate, **Karen McNamara**, won the seat.

---

# Important NSW contests

## Warringah

- Won by **Tony Abbott**, Liberal leader.
- Abbott became **Prime Minister of Australia** after the election.
- Warringah was a safe Liberal seat on Sydney’s northern beaches.

## Grayndler

- Won by **Anthony Albanese** for Labor.
- Albanese became Labor’s deputy leader after the election and later became Labor leader and Prime Minister in 2022.

## Wentworth

- Won by **Malcolm Turnbull** for the Liberals.
- Turnbull later became Prime Minister in 2015.

## North Sydney

- Won by **Joe Hockey**.
- Hockey became Treasurer in the Abbott government.

## Cook

- Won by **Scott Morrison**.
- Morrison became Minister for Immigration and Border Protection after the election and later Prime Minister in 2018.

## New England

- Won by **Barnaby Joyce** for the Nationals.
- This was a major National Party gain after Tony Windsor retired.

## Lyne

- Won by **David Gillespie** for the Nationals.
- The seat returned to the Nationals after Rob Oakeshott retired.

## Eden-Monaro

- Won by **Peter Hendy** for the Liberals.
- Eden-Monaro was famous as a bellwether seat, having often gone with the party forming government.

## Robertson

- Won by **Lucy Wicks** for the Liberals.
- A key Central Coast marginal seat.

## Lindsay

- Won by **Fiona Scott** for the Liberals.
- A high-profile western Sydney gain from Labor.

---

# Senate result in New South Wales

Six Senate positions were contested in NSW.

The elected senators were:

| Senator elected | Party |
|---|---|
| Concetta Fierravanti-Wells | Liberal Party |
| John Williams | National Party |
| Arthur Sinodinos | Liberal Party |
| Doug Cameron | Australian Labor Party |
| Sam Dastyari | Australian Labor Party |
| David Leyonhjelm | Liberal Democratic Party |

The Senate result was notable because **David Leyonhjelm** of the **Liberal Democratic Party** was elected. His party received a surprisingly high vote in NSW, helped in part by its position on the large Senate ballot paper and possible confusion among some voters between the Liberal Party and the Liberal Democratic Party.

The Greens did **not** win one of the six NSW Senate seats at this election, although Greens senator Lee Rhiannon continued in the Senate because she had been elected at the previous half-Senate election.

---

## Senate seats won by party in NSW

| Party/group | Senate seats won |
|---|---:|
| Liberal/National Coalition | 3 |
| Labor | 2 |
| Liberal Democratic Party | 1 |
| Greens | 0 |
| **Total** | **6** |

---

# Political significance of the NSW result

The NSW result was crucial to the Coalition’s national victory.

Key points:

1. **The Coalition dominated NSW**, winning 30 of 48 lower-house seats.
2. **Labor suffered heavy losses**, particularly in western Sydney and marginal regional seats.
3. **The Nationals recovered former independent seats**, especially New England and Lyne.
4. **Western Sydney was central to the Coalition campaign**, with seats such as Lindsay, Banks, Reid and Barton falling to the Liberals.
5. Several major national figures represented NSW seats, including Tony Abbott, Malcolm Turnbull, Scott Morrison, Joe Hockey, Anthony Albanese, Tanya Plibersek and Chris Bowen.
6. The NSW Senate result produced one of the election’s most surprising outcomes: the election of Liberal Democrat David Leyonhjelm.

---

In summary, the **2013 federal election in New South Wales** was a decisive Coalition victory. The Liberal and National parties won a combined **30 seats**, Labor was reduced to **18**, and the Coalition secured important gains across western Sydney, the Central Coast and regional NSW. The result helped deliver Tony Abbott a comfortable national majority and played a central role in the change of government.
